claim: Fluctuations in organelle abundance can profoundly limit the precision of cell biological processes from secretion to metabolism.
source: Fluctuations in organelle abundance can profoundly limit the precision of cell biological processes from secretion to metabolism.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is presented as a premise for the study, drawing on general scientific understanding.

claim: The model exactly predicts the size of experimentally measured Golgi apparatus and vacuole abundance fluctuations.
source: Our model exactly predicts the size of experimentally measured Golgi apparatus and vacuole abundance fluctuations, suggesting that cells tolerate the maximum level of variability generated by the Golgi and vacuole biogenesis pathways.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 2C, 2D, 2G, 2H).

claim: Cells tolerate the maximum level of variability generated by the Golgi and vacuole biogenesis pathways.
source: Our model exactly predicts the size of experimentally measured Golgi apparatus and vacuole abundance fluctuations, suggesting that cells tolerate the maximum level of variability generated by the Golgi and vacuole biogenesis pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the close match between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements without invoking feedback control mechanisms.

claim: Large increases in peroxisome abundance fluctuations are observed when cells are transferred from glucose-rich to fatty acid-rich environments.
source: We observe large increases in peroxisome abundance fluctuations when cells are transferred from glucose-rich to fatty acid-rich environments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Increased peroxisome abundance fluctuations in fatty acid-rich environments are significantly diminished in mutants lacking peroxisome fission factors.
source: These increased fluctuations are significantly diminished in mutants lacking peroxisome fission factors, leading us to infer that peroxisome biogenesis switches from de novo synthesis to primarily fission.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Peroxisome biogenesis switches from de novo synthesis to primarily fission when cells are transferred to fatty acid-rich environments.
source: These increased fluctuations are significantly diminished in mutants lacking peroxisome fission factors, leading us to infer that peroxisome biogenesis switches from de novo synthesis to primarily fission.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fission mutants show reduced fluctuations in oleic acid medium.

claim: Stochasticity in the abundance of cellular components is an intrinsic feature of biological systems.
source: Stochasticity in the abundance of cellular components is an intrinsic feature of biological systems.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Noise in molecular-scale processes such as gene expression and signal transduction have been examined in great detail.
source: But while noise in molecular-scale processes such as gene expression and signal transduction have been examined in great detail, fluctuations have not been systematically characterized at one of the most critical scales of biological organization: compartmentalization of the eukaryotic cell into organelles.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Fluctuations have not been systematically characterized at the scale of organelle compartmentalization.
source: But while noise in molecular-scale processes such as gene expression and signal transduction have been examined in great detail, fluctuations have not been systematically characterized at one of the most critical scales of biological organization: compartmentalization of the eukaryotic cell into organelles.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: It has been suggested that the cell may be able to count and tightly control the number of a given organelle.
source: It has been suggested, for example, that the cell may be able to count and tightly control the number of a given organelle (Rafelski and Marshall, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There is a lack of comparisons of theoretical calculations of cell-to-cell variability in organelle abundances to experimentally measured organelle abundance distributions.
source: However, we lack comparisons of theoretical calculations of cell-to-cell variability in organelle abundances to experimentally measured organelle abundance distributions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: There are four basic processes resulting in organelle abundance changes: de novo synthesis, fission, fusion, and decay.
source: There are four basic processes resulting in organelle abundance changes that can give rise to fluctuations in organelle number: de novo synthesis from a pre-existing membrane source, fission (Lowe and Barr, 2007), fusion (Denesvre and Malhotra, 1996), and decay such as through partitioning during cell division or autophagy (van der Vaart et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Golgi abundance is the result of a steady-state determined by the balance of de novo synthesis and decay through maturation and dilution by cell division.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Golgi abundance is the result of a steady-state determined by the balance of de novo synthesis and decay through maturation and dilution by cell division (Rossanese et al., 1999; Bevis et al., 2002; Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006);
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Modest levels of Golgi fusion have been reported.
source: though modest levels of Golgi fusion have been reported (Bhave et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Golgi decay appears to be dominated by maturation.
source: decay appears to be dominated by maturation (Losev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Vacuolar abundance is thought to be primarily determined by the balance of fission and fusion events.
source: Vacuolar abundance is thought to be primarily determined by the balance of fission and fusion events (Wickner, 2002),
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Vacuoles can be generated de novo in mutant yeast strains with impaired vacuole inheritance pathways.
source: though vacuoles can be generated de novo in mutant yeast strains with impaired vacuole inheritance pathways (Banta et al., 1988; Catlett and Weisman, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The quantitative contribution of de novo vacuole biogenesis to vacuole copy number remains uncharacterized in physiological conditions.
source: the quantitative contribution of de novo vacuole biogenesis to vacuole copy number remains uncharacterized in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Peroxisomes are thought to increase in number by both de novo synthesis and fission pathways.
source: Peroxisomes, for example, are thought to increase in number by both de novo synthesis (Hoepfner et al., 2005; van der Zand et al., 2012) and fission pathways (Hoepfner et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2005; Motley and Hettema, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mature peroxisomes do not undergo fusion events.
source: Mature peroxisomes do not undergo fusion events (Motley and Hettema, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Peroxisome abundances can be actively upregulated by culturing budding yeast cells in medium containing long chain fatty acids such as oleic acid.
source: Furthermore, peroxisome abundances can be actively upregulated by culturing budding yeast cells in medium containing long chain fatty acids such as oleic acid (Mast et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There is a lack of quantitative understanding of whether de novo synthesis or fission dominates the generation of peroxisomes in steady growth in glucose or during active proliferation in oleic acid.
source: We lack a quantitative understanding of whether de novo synthesis or fission dominates the generation of peroxisomes in either steady growth in glucose or during active proliferation in oleic acid.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: The Fano factor is the variance of the distribution divided by the mean of the distribution.
source: To compare the variances of the distributions from different simulation regimes, we calculated the variance of the distribution divided by the mean of the distribution, also known as the Fano factor.
evidence: This is a definition from statistical theory.

claim: The Fano factor equals 1 for a Poisson distribution.
source: We chose to work with the Fano factor, rather than alternative metrics for fluctuations such as the coefficient of variation, because it equals 1 for a Poisson distribution, and so we can readily detect the deviations from Poisson statistics that arise from fission and fusion mediated processes by comparing the observed Fano factor to 1.
evidence: This is a known property of the Poisson distribution from statistical theory.

claim: Paulsson (2005) showed that the Fano factor for a given reaction scheme can be approximately calculated according to a restatement of the fluctuation dissipation theorem.
source: Building on earlier work from the theory of stochastic processes, Paulsson (2005) showed that the Fano factor for a given reaction scheme can be approximately calculated according to a restatement of the fluctuation dissipation theorem:
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The analytical expression for the Fano factor yields a quantity that increases with an increase in the ratio of the rates of fission and de novo synthesis.
source: Consistent with our simulation results, the analytical expression for the Fano factor yields a quantity that increases with an increase in the ratio of the rates of fission and de novo synthesis, but decreases with an increase in the rate of fusion (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by the analytical calculation and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The analytical expression for the Fano factor yields a quantity that decreases with an increase in the rate of fusion.
source: Consistent with our simulation results, the analytical expression for the Fano factor yields a quantity that increases with an increase in the ratio of the rates of fission and de novo synthesis, but decreases with an increase in the rate of fusion (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by the analytical calculation and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: If the mean organelle abundance is larger than 1, the difference between the exact Fano factor obtained from simulation and the result of Equation 1 virtually disappears.
source: As shown in Figure 1I, no matter which rate constant is varied, if the mean organelle abundance is larger than 1 then the difference between the exact Fano factor obtained from simulation and the result of Equation 1 virtually disappears.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of analytical and simulation results shown in Figure 1I.

claim: For the Golgi apparatus, kfusion = kfission = 0 as the Golgi apparatus is only affected by de novo synthesis and decay through maturation in budding yeast.
source: In case 1, corresponding to the Golgi apparatus, kfusion = kfission = 0 as the Golgi apparatus is only affected by de novo synthesis and decay through maturation in budding yeast (Rossanese et al., 1999; Bevis et al., 2002; Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: When kfusion = kfission = 0, Equation 1 reduces to σ2/<n> = 1.
source: In this limit Equation 1 reduces to σ2/<n> = 1, reflecting the fact that de novo synthesis and first order decay operating alone corresponds to a Poisson process;
evidence: This is derived from the analytical model.

claim: De novo synthesis and first order decay operating alone corresponds to a Poisson process.
source: In this limit Equation 1 reduces to σ2/<n> = 1, reflecting the fact that de novo synthesis and first order decay operating alone corresponds to a Poisson process;
evidence: This is a known result from stochastic process theory.

claim: One of the hallmarks of the Poisson distribution is that its variance equals its mean.
source: one of the hallmarks of the Poisson distribution is that its variance equals its mean, and our approximate equation for the Fano factor reduces exactly to this limit.
evidence: This is a known property of the Poisson distribution from statistical theory.

claim: The Golgi abundance distribution should yield a Fano factor of 1.
source: Thus, we would expect that the Golgi abundance distribution should yield a Fano factor of 1.
evidence: This is predicted from the theoretical model.

claim: The measured Golgi abundance distribution closely matches the Poisson distribution derived from the experimentally determined mean Golgi abundance.
source: We see excellent agreement between the theory and experiment, as the measured Golgi abundance distribution closely matches the Poisson distribution derived from the experimentally determined mean Golgi abundance (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The measured Golgi abundance distribution Fano factor is σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.1.
source: and we measure a Fano factor σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.1 (Figure 2D, red bar), in agreement with the theoretically predicted σ2/<n> = 1 (Figure 2D, blue bar).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The late Golgi abundance distribution closely matches a Poisson distribution.
source: Interestingly, when we repeat these measurements for the late Golgi by performing confocal microscopy on a budding yeast strain expressing the green fluorescent protein (GFP) fused to the late Golgi marker protein Sec7, we see virtually identical results with the late Golgi abundance distribution closely matching a Poisson distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The measured late Golgi Fano factor is σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.1.
source: and thus yielding a measured Fano factor of σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Synchronizing the cell cycle phases of cells by arresting them in S-phase does not affect the Fano factors of the measured abundance distributions for the Golgi or late Golgi.
source: We see that synchronizing the cell cycle phases of the cells we examine by microscopy does not affect the Fano factors of the measured abundance distributions for the Golgi or late Golgi (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: For the vacuole, kde novo = γ = 0 as the vacuole is only affected by fission and fusion.
source: In case 2, corresponding to the vacuole, kde novo = γ = 0 as the vacuole is only affected by fission and fusion (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on the established understanding of vacuole biogenesis and illustrated in Figure 2E.

claim: The experimentally measured mean number of vacuoles is 2.1.
source: Given an experimentally measured mean number of vacuoles of 2.1 (Wickner, 2002; 'Materials and methods'),
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and the Materials and methods section.

claim: The predicted vacuole distribution Fano factor is σ2/<n> = 0.5.
source: we make the non-trivial prediction that σ2/<n> = 0.5 for the vacuole distribution.
evidence: This is predicted from the theoretical model using the experimentally measured mean.

claim: A Fano factor of less than 1 resulting from fission and fusion processes operating together is purely due to the low numbers of vacuoles present at steady state.
source: This is a surprising and strong prediction of the model because a Fano factor of less than 1 resulting from fission and fusion processes operating together is purely due to the low numbers of vacuoles present at steady state;
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model.

claim: If the mean vacuole number were much larger than 1, then the Fano factor would approach 1 and be indistinguishable from case 1.
source: if <n> were much larger than 1, then the Fano factor would approach 1 and be indistinguishable from case 1.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model.

claim: Vacuole abundance follows a shifted Poisson distribution.
source: This distinction between case 1 and case 2 is a reflection of the fact that vacuole abundance, the result of a balance between fission and fusion events, follows a shifted Poisson distribution.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model.

claim: In a shifted Poisson distribution, the probability of having n = 0 vacuoles is 0 because a cell can only reduce its vacuole numbers through fusion events to n = 1 vacuole, at which point the fusion rate kfusion n(n-1) = 0.
source: In a shifted Poisson distribution, the probability of having n = 0 vacuoles is 0 because a cell can only reduce its vacuole numbers through fusion events to n = 1 vacuole, at which point the fusion rate kfusion n(n-1) = 0.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model and the properties of the shifted Poisson distribution.

claim: The measured vacuole abundance distribution overlaps with the theoretically predicted shifted Poisson distribution.
source: We see an excellent match between theory and experiment; we observe a distribution overlapping with the theoretically predicted shifted Poisson distribution (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The measured vacuole Fano factor is σ2/<n> = 0.5 ± 0.1.
source: and measure a Fano factor σ2/<n> = 0.5 ± 0.1 (Figure 2H, red bar), in agreement with the theoretically predicted σ2/<n> = 0.5 (Figure 2H, blue bar);
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The close match between theory and experiment for vacuoles suggests that de novo vacuole biogenesis does not play a quantitatively significant role in affecting vacuole abundance in wild-type yeast.
source: It is important to note that the close match between theory and experiment here suggests that de novo vacuole biogenesis, which is observed only in mutant strains that specifically disable vacuole inheritance, appears not to play a quantitatively significant role in affecting vacuole abundance in wild-type yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the close match between theoretical predictions (which assume no de novo biogenesis) and experimental measurements.

claim: Budding yeast cells tolerate the maximum level of variability generated by the biogenesis pathways governing Golgi apparatus and vacuole abundance.
source: First, budding yeast cells tolerate the maximum level of variability generated by the biogenesis pathways governing Golgi apparatus and vacuole abundance, evidenced by the fact that our model predicted the experimental data with high quantitative accuracy without invoking any feedback control mechanisms to control the number of organelles.
evidence: This is inferred from the close match between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements without invoking feedback control.

claim: Different biogenesis mechanisms generate differing levels of abundance fluctuations.
source: Second, as expected from theory, different biogenesis mechanisms generate differing levels of abundance fluctuations.
evidence: This is supported by the theoretical model and experimental data comparing Golgi and vacuole fluctuations.

claim: At low mean organelle copy numbers, organelles governed by fission and fusion (vacuole) inherently exhibit smaller abundance fluctuations than organelles governed by de novo synthesis and decay (Golgi).
source: At low mean organelle copy numbers, organelles governed by fission and fusion (vacuole; Figure 2H) inherently exhibit smaller abundance fluctuations than organelles governed by de novo synthesis and decay (Golgi; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2H.

claim: Even though up to 50% of the vacuole membrane is generated de novo in a given cell, actual vacuole copy number is likely not strongly affected by de novo vacuole biogenesis.
source: In particular, even though up to 50% of the vacuole membrane is generated de novo in a given cell (Catlett and Weisman, 2000), actual vacuole copy number is likely not strongly affected by de novo vacuole biogenesis, consistent with the most widely accepted model of vacuole biogenesis (Wickner, 2002).
evidence: This is inferred from the fluctuation analysis and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For peroxisomes, fusion is thought to be negligible and Equation 1 reduces to σ2/<n> = 1 + kfission<n>/kde novo.
source: In case 3, corresponding to the peroxisome, fusion is thought to be negligible and Equation 1 reduces to σ2〈n〉=1+kfission〈n〉kde novo (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is derived from the analytical model and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: A Fano factor significantly larger than 1 indicates that fission dominates over de novo synthesis in generating an increased number of organelles.
source: Specifically, in the absence of fusion, a Fano factor significantly larger than 1 indicates that fission dominates over de novo synthesis in generating an increased number of organelles, while a Fano factor close to 1 indicates that de novo synthesis dominates over fission.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model.

claim: A Fano factor close to 1 indicates that de novo synthesis dominates over fission.
source: Specifically, in the absence of fusion, a Fano factor significantly larger than 1 indicates that fission dominates over de novo synthesis in generating an increased number of organelles, while a Fano factor close to 1 indicates that de novo synthesis dominates over fission.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model.

claim: If de novo synthesis dominates over fission, the organelle abundance distribution will closely match a Poisson distribution.
source: Furthermore, if de novo synthesis dominates over fission, we also expect to see that the organelle abundance distribution will closely match a Poisson distribution, as we observed for the Golgi apparatus, while if fission dominates then we expect a distribution broader than Poisson.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model.

claim: If fission dominates, the organelle abundance distribution is expected to be broader than Poisson.
source: Furthermore, if de novo synthesis dominates over fission, we also expect to see that the organelle abundance distribution will closely match a Poisson distribution, as we observed for the Golgi apparatus, while if fission dominates then we expect a distribution broader than Poisson.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model.

claim: Peroxisomes are greatly upregulated in number when yeast cells are cultured in fatty acid-rich medium.
source: Notably, peroxisomes are greatly upregulated in number when yeast cells are cultured in fatty acid-rich medium;
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The simplified peroxisome biogenesis model is statistically equivalent to the more detailed model of de novo peroxisome biogenesis that explicitly tracks the creation and fusion dynamics of Pex2/10 and Pex13/14 containing vesicles.
source: From this result we conclude that our original simple, one-step de novo biogenesis pathway model is statistically equivalent to the more detailed model of de novo peroxisome biogenesis that explicitly tracks the creation and fusion dynamics of Pex2/10 and Pex13/14 containing vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the two models shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Fano factor for the peroxisome abundance distribution for cells cultured in glucose is σ2/<n> = 1.1 ± 0.1.
source: After measuring single cell histograms of peroxisomes (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), we calculate that the Fano factors for the peroxisome abundance distributions for cells cultured in glucose is σ2/<n> = 1.1 ± 0.1 (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C),
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, 2C.

claim: Peroxisomes are generated primarily by de novo synthesis in glucose.
source: leading us to infer that the organelle is generated primarily by de novo synthesis in glucose.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured Fano factor being close to 1.

claim: In cells cultured in oleic acid-containing medium, there is a marked increase in the size of the organelle abundance fluctuations for peroxisomes.
source: In cells cultured in oleic acid-containing medium, however, we see a marked increase in the size of the organelle abundance fluctuations for peroxisomes (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B),
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The measured peroxisome Fano factor in oleic acid-containing medium is σ2/<n> = 2.4 ± 0.2.
source: with a measured Fano factor of σ2/<n> = 2.4 ± 0.2 (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Increased pre-peroxisomal vesicle production and fusion cannot explain the rise in the mature peroxisome abundance distribution Fano factor obtained from cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: Therefore, we conclude that increased pre-peroxisomal vesicle production and fusion cannot explain the rise in the mature peroxisome abundance distribution Fano factor obtained from cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
evidence: This is inferred from simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Upon transfer to oleic acid containing medium, budding yeast cells primarily generate new peroxisomes by fission of pre-existing peroxisomes.
source: Instead we infer that upon transfer to oleic acid containing medium budding yeast cells primarily generate new peroxisomes by fission of pre-existing peroxisomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased Fano factor in oleic acid medium.

claim: For the Golgi apparatus, the Fano factor remains virtually unchanged at σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.2 in oleic acid rich medium.
source: We confirm that for the Golgi apparatus the Fano factor remains virtually unchanged at σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.2 while for the vacuole the Fano factor increases to σ2/<n> = 0.8 ± 0.1 respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: For the vacuole, the Fano factor increases to σ2/<n> = 0.8 ± 0.1 in oleic acid rich medium.
source: We confirm that for the Golgi apparatus the Fano factor remains virtually unchanged at σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.2 while for the vacuole the Fano factor increases to σ2/<n> = 0.8 ± 0.1 respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The rise in the vacuole abundance distribution Fano factor is consistent with the increase in mean vacuole abundance in oleic acid cultured cells from <n> = 2.1 to <n> = 4.0.
source: This rise in the vacuole abundance distribution Fano factor is consistent with the increase in mean vacuole abundance in oleic acid cultured cells from <n> = 2.1 to <n> = 4.0.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model and experimental data.

claim: Organelle sizes scale with cellular volume and ploidy.
source: We conjectured, motivated by the observation that organelle sizes scale with cellular volume and ploidy (Weiss et al., 1975; Chan and Marshall, 2010; Uchida et al., 2011), that diploid cells may have higher mean numbers of organelles,
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Vacuole and peroxisome abundance distributions have increased means in diploid cells compared to haploid cells.
source: We found that vacuole and peroxisome abundance distributions have increased means in diploid cells compared to haploid cells;
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4E.

claim: The Golgi apparatus and late Golgi did not yield a statistically significant increase in mean abundance in diploid cells.
source: the Golgi apparatus and late Golgi notably did not yield a statistically significant increase in mean abundance in diploid cells (Figure 4—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: In diploid cells, the mean vacuole abundance is <n> = 3.6, which represents a 71% increase from the haploid value of 2.1.
source: In the case of the diploid vacuole abundance distribution, <n> = 3.6, which represents a 71% increase from the haploid value of 2.1 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The diploid vacuole abundance distribution is well described by a shifted Poisson distribution calculated from the experimentally measured mean.
source: The diploid vacuole abundance distribution is still well described by a shifted Poisson distribution that is calculated from the experimentally measured mean, again with no fitting parameters (Figure 4A, blue line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When the vacuole mean is <n> = 3.6, the predicted Fano factor is σ2/<n> = 0.7.
source: Our equation for the Fano factor predicts that when the vacuole mean is <n> = 3.6, the Fano factor σ2〈n〉=1−1〈n〉=0.7, higher than the prediction in the haploid case of σ2/<n> = 0.5.
evidence: This is predicted from the theoretical model.

claim: In diploid cells expressing Vph1-GFP, the measured vacuole Fano factor is σ2/<n> = 0.7 ± 0.1.
source: In diploid cells expressing the Vph1-GFP marker we measure a Fano factor of σ2/<n> = 0.7 ± 0.1, significantly higher than the haploid value of σ2/<n> = 0.5 ± 0.1 (Figure 4C), and consistent with our theoretical prediction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In diploid cells cultured in glucose-rich medium, the mean peroxisome abundance is <n> = 6.8, representing roughly a doubling compared to haploid cells.
source: In the case of peroxisomes, the diploid organelle abundance distributions yield <n> = 6.8, respectively, when cells are cultured in glucose-rich medium, representing roughly a doubling in mean abundance in each case compared to the haploid abundance distributions (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The diploid peroxisome abundance distribution closely matches the Poisson distribution derived from the experimentally measured mean.
source: We calculated the Poisson distribution derived from the experimentally measured mean abundances and find that the predicted distributions, even with no fitting parameters, closely describe the experimentally measured abundance distributions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The measured peroxisome Fano factor in diploid cells cultured in glucose is σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.1.
source: The measured Fano factor matches the theoretical prediction closely at σ2/<n> = 1.0 ± 0.1 for the peroxisome (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The Fano factors for the peroxisome abundance distribution in diploid cells grown in glucose are much smaller than the Fano factors measured in cells grown in oleic acid-rich medium despite similar mean values.
source: Interestingly, the Fano factors for the peroxisome abundance distribution in diploid cells grown in glucose are much smaller than the Fano factors measured in cells grown in oleic acid-rich medium (Figure 4F) despite the fact that their mean values are similar (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: The difference in Fano factors between diploid cells in glucose and cells in oleic acid provides additional evidence that peroxisome biogenesis involves fundamentally different mechanisms in glucose-cultured cells vs oleic acid-cultured cells.
source: This provides additional evidence that peroxisome biogenesis involves fundamentally different mechanisms in glucose-cultured cells vs oleic acid-cultured cells, with our model pointing to the less noisy de novo synthesis pathway dominating the former and the more noisy fission pathway dominating the latter.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Fano factors.

claim: Peroxisome fission is mediated by the proteins Vps1, Dnm1 and its accessory protein Fis1, with the dominant role played by Vps1.
source: Peroxisome fission is mediated by the proteins Vps1, Dnm1 and its accessory protein Fis1, with the dominant role played by Vps1 (Kuravi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mean peroxisome abundance decreases by fourfold in vps1Δ cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: We find that the mean peroxisome abundance decreases by fourfold in vps1Δ cells, while the peroxisome abundance distribution Fano factor is reduced threefold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The peroxisome abundance distribution Fano factor is reduced threefold in vps1Δ cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: We find that the mean peroxisome abundance decreases by fourfold in vps1Δ cells, while the peroxisome abundance distribution Fano factor is reduced threefold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mean peroxisome abundance decreases by slightly less than twofold in fis1Δ cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: As expected, the effects in fis1Δ and dnm1Δ cells are weaker: the mean peroxisome abundance decreases by slightly less than twofold in fis1Δ cells and roughly 10% in dnm1Δ cells,
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mean peroxisome abundance decreases by roughly 10% in dnm1Δ cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: As expected, the effects in fis1Δ and dnm1Δ cells are weaker: the mean peroxisome abundance decreases by slightly less than twofold in fis1Δ cells and roughly 10% in dnm1Δ cells,
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Fano factor for fis1Δ cells is reduced by ∼30% compared to wild-type cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: while the Fano factors for fis1Δ and dnm1Δ cells are reduced by ∼30% and ∼15% respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Fano factor for dnm1Δ cells is reduced by ∼15% compared to wild-type cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: while the Fano factors for fis1Δ and dnm1Δ cells are reduced by ∼30% and ∼15% respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Fano factor measured for vps1Δ cells is σ2/<n> = 1.0, exactly what one would expect for de novo synthesis dominated peroxisome production.
source: Most importantly, the Fano factor measured for vps1Δ cells is σ2/<n> = 1.0, exactly what one would expect for de novo synthesis dominated peroxisome production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fission dominates peroxisome proliferation in wild-type cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
source: These results strongly suggest that fission dominates peroxisome proliferation in wild-type cells cultured in oleic acid medium.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on fission mutants.

claim: Budding yeast cells tolerate the theoretically predicted maximum Fano factors consistent with the known mechanisms of Golgi apparatus and vacuole biogenesis.
source: Our results show that budding yeast cells tolerate the theoretically predicted maximum Fano factors consistent with the known mechanisms of Golgi apparatus and vacuole biogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the close match between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements.

claim: The peroxisome abundance distribution is consistent with a model in which the organelle is created primarily by de novo synthesis in glucose-cultured budding yeast cells.
source: Our results showed that the peroxisome abundance distribution is consistent with a model in which the organelle is created primarily by de novo synthesis in glucose-cultured budding yeast cells, but then switch to a noisy, fission-dominated biogenesis when cells are cultured in a fatty acid rich environment in which organelle biogenesis is upregulated.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured Fano factors.

claim: Peroxisomes switch to a noisy, fission-dominated biogenesis when cells are cultured in a fatty acid rich environment.
source: Our results showed that the peroxisome abundance distribution is consistent with a model in which the organelle is created primarily by de novo synthesis in glucose-cultured budding yeast cells, but then switch to a noisy, fission-dominated biogenesis when cells are cultured in a fatty acid rich environment in which organelle biogenesis is upregulated.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured Fano factors.

claim: The close match between the model and measurements without invoking feedback control implies that cells tolerate the maximum amount of variability in endomembrane organelle abundance generated by a given set of biogenesis mechanisms.
source: While some subcellular structures such as the nucleus and centrioles are clearly under the control of strong feedback control mechanisms that suppress fluctuations in their abundances (Marshall, 2007), the cell apparently tolerates the maximum amount of variability in endomembrane organelle abundance generated by a given set of biogenesis mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the close match between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements without invoking feedback control.

claim: The nucleus and centrioles are under the control of strong feedback control mechanisms that suppress fluctuations in their abundances.
source: While some subcellular structures such as the nucleus and centrioles are clearly under the control of strong feedback control mechanisms that suppress fluctuations in their abundances (Marshall, 2007),
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The rate of peroxisome decay via autophagy depends on the existence of a functional fission pathway.
source: For example, it has been recently shown that the rate of peroxisome decay via autophagy depends on the existence of a functional fission pathway (Mao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Peroxisomes are created de novo in glucose-rich conditions.
source: Our results suggest a resolution to the long-running debate over whether peroxisome biogenesis is the result of de novo synthesis or fission (Hoepfner et al., 2005; Motley and Hettema, 2007; Mast et al., 2010; van der Zand et al., 2012), with our theory and measurements supporting a model in which peroxisomes are created de novo in glucose-rich conditions, but switch to primarily fission-based proliferation in fatty acid rich environments that demand peroxisomal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Fano factors and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Peroxisomes switch to primarily fission-based proliferation in fatty acid rich environments.
source: Our results suggest a resolution to the long-running debate over whether peroxisome biogenesis is the result of de novo synthesis or fission (Hoepfner et al., 2005; Motley and Hettema, 2007; Mast et al., 2010; van der Zand et al., 2012), with our theory and measurements supporting a model in which peroxisomes are created de novo in glucose-rich conditions, but switch to primarily fission-based proliferation in fatty acid rich environments that demand peroxisomal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Fano factors and supported by citations to prior work.

source: All strains were taken from the collection of GFP fusion strains generated by Huh et al. (2003).

claim: Anp1-mRFP forms punctate spots marking the presence of individual Golgi.
source: Anp1-mRFP forms punctate spots (Figure 2B) marking the presence of individual Golgi, whose number we quantified in each cell to generate a Golgi abundance histogram from which we could calculate the Fano factor.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Vph1-GFP forms discrete rings marking vacuoles.
source: Vph1-GFP forms discrete rings (Figure 2F) that we count in each cell to construct vacuole abundance distributions, as was done for the Golgi.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 2F.
